title: When someone mocks
hookLine: responding to mockery of the turban with calm and courage
tomorrow: next summer's camp form came. will Simran come back from college?

cards: Hot face. Tight jaw. Hands that want to do something.
Simran is still feeling all three at pickup, telling Bebe what happened at lunch. Gurveer wore his new turban to school for the first time.

A boy at the next table called it a tomato, reached over to flick it, and half the table laughed. Simran has seen this before, with Fateh's patka, and this time she wants to go back in and flip that table.
Bebe puts a hand on her arm and says a line from Baba Farid instead.

teach.h: FARID: ANGER MAKES THE BODY SICK.
teach.b: Farid's salok, on ang 1381, says, in paraphrase: answer evil with goodness, and don't let anger fill your mind; then your body won't fall sick. Notice he starts with the body.
The heat Simran feels is real, and Farid's point is that anger left to run will make you ill before it fixes anything.
But calm isn't the same as doing nothing. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok on ang 1427 gives the other half. In paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is afraid of no one, call that one wise.

teach.h: FRIGHTEN NO ONE. FEAR NO ONE.
teach.b: Don't frighten anyone: no flipped tables, no threats back. Don't be afraid: Gurveer doesn't have to take the turban off, or laugh along as if it's nothing. So that evening, on a call, they practice.
Gurveer sits up, breathes out, and says in an ordinary voice: it's my dastar. I tied it myself this morning.

That's calm courage, out loud. And Simran does her part the same way: the next day she goes with him to the school counselor, firm and unhurried. If teasing turns to pushing or threats, the adults step in.
Calm courage never means putting up with harm.

how: Sikh families teach young people to answer mockery of the turban or patka calmly and plainly, to explain what it is, and to tell a trusted adult; parents and older siblings speak to schools when it continues.

o: staying silent and walking away from every insult
answering ridicule with a steady body and a clear voice
the right to strike back when someone insults the Guru

games.q: calm and courage — tap the pairs.
p: frighten no one, fear no one
it's my dastar. I tied it myself.

s: staying calm when mocked means saying nothing and letting it go
Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok pairs frightening no one with being afraid of no one. Gurveer says it out loud.
Farid's salok links anger to the body falling sick
on ang 1381: don't let anger fill your mind, and your body won't fall sick.
calm courage means handling bullying alone
if teasing turns to pushing or threats, the adults step in.

games.q: a coworker keeps making jokes about your accent in meetings. going by today, what's the move?
o: laugh along so it looks like it doesn't bother you.
snap back in front of everyone so they never try it again.
steady your breath, then say plainly, without heat, that it isn't okay.
games.why: frighten no one, fear no one: no counterattack, no hiding. a steady body first, then a clear voice.

practice: Sit tall with both feet flat on the floor. Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, and rest one hand on your chest. Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in, and feel the heat settle without letting your back slump.

wordCard.voice: When someone mocks. Answering with a steady body and a clear voice: frightening no one, afraid of no one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nirbhau, without fear; a word from the Mool Mantar describing God.

carryVoice: Calm courage: the jaw unclenched, the voice clear, and the turban still on. See you tomorrow.
